result.markdown: # Foundational data frame subsetting ![](/images/subset_table.png){style="width:200px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} __Data frames__ can be subset similar to __vectors__. As with __vectors__ you can use `[]`. Additionally, `$` can be used to subset __data frames__. Square brackets must be provided indexes for rows and for columns. The structure for this is `df[row,column]`. It is very useful to remember that R always wants rows first then columns second. ## Read in Parks biodiversity data frame ![](/images/biodiversity.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} To practice subsetting __data frames__ with square brackets we will __read__ in a new file called [parks_biodiveristy.csv](https://neof-workshops.github.io/R_j4c0xh/downloads/parks_biodiveristy.csv). This contains the number of different species of various groups (Bird, Mammal, etc.) in US national parks. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #Read in the file parks_df <- read.csv("parks_biodiveristy.csv", check.names = FALSE, row.names = 1) #View the resulting object parks_df #View its column names colnames(parks_df) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="parks_biodiveristy.csv source"} Original data can be found: ::: ## Square bracket subsetting ![](/images/R_square_bracket.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"} Now for some subset commands specifying the row/s then column/s with square brackets (`[]`). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #Scalar from the 1st row and 1st column parks_df[1,1] #Row names and column names can be used for indexing #Scalar from the row called YOSE and the column called Amphibian parks_df["YOSE","Amphibian"] #More examples parks_df[1:10,2] parks_df[1:10,"State"] parks_df[3,2:4] parks_df["SAGU",2] parks_df[1:10,"Bird"] parks_df[c(1,3,5,6),c("Bird","Fish")] ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Rows then columns A quick reminder that it is always rows then columns in square brackets. `df[row,column]` ::: ## Subsetted object As you can see in the above set of code the structure of the resulting subsetted object is dependant on how it was subsetted. It may be a __scalar__, __vector__, or __data frame__. Below describes what structure your resulting subsetted object will be based on the subsetting. - __Scalar__: - Indexing to get a single value by choosing one row and one column - E.g. `parks_df[1,1]` - __Vector__: - Indexing so you get multiple values from one column - This occurs as each column is in essence a __vector__ - E.g. `parks_df[1:10,2]` - __Data frame__: - Indexing so you get multiple values from a row or multiple columns - Subsetting a __data frame__ like this provides you with a __data frame__ - E.g. `parks_df[3,2:4]` or `parks_df[3:4,2:4]` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: :::
